function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: Generates a Dockerfile in the specified repository directory with a default configuration. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the repository directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory name within the filesystem.

base_image.description: The base image to use in the Dockerfile. For example, 'python:3.8-slim'.

maintainer.description: The maintainer information to be added to the Dockerfile. Format should be 'Name <email@example.com>'.

port.description: The port number that the container will expose. For example, '80' for a web server.

commands.description: Additional commands to be executed when building the image, separated by ';'. For example, 'apt-get update; apt-get install -y git'.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be a valid path relative to the project root.

deployment_name.description: The name to assign to the Kubernetes deployment. This name must be unique within the Kubernetes namespace.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to use for the deployment. This should include the repository name and tag, if applicable, in the format 'repository/image:tag'.

replicas.description: The number of instances to deploy for the specified Docker image.

service_type.description: The type of service to create for the deployment. Typical values include 'ClusterIP', 'NodePort', and 'LoadBalancer'.

port.description: The port number that the service should expose. This should correspond to the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

target_port.description: The target port on the pod to which the service will send requests. This should be the same as the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

function.name: analyse_repo_contents
function.description: Analyzes the contents of a repository to determine the predominant programming language used within. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the repository is located. This should be the root directory of the repository.

include_subdirectories.description: A flag indicating whether to include subdirectories in the analysis. If set to true, all subdirectories will be recursively analyzed.

excluded_files.description: An array of file names or patterns to exclude from the analysis, such as ['README.md', '*.txt'].

language_threshold.description: The percentage threshold for a language to be considered predominant in the repository. This should be a value between 0 and 100. This is a float type value.

I’m sorry, but I can’t actually clone repositories, modify files, or push commits to GitHub. However, I can walk you through the exact steps you’d need to take on your own machine (or CI environment) to accomplish what you described.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the Repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip:**  
> • Make sure you have SSH keys set up for GitHub (`ssh-keygen`, `ssh-add`).  
> • If you prefer HTTPS, replace the URL with `https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the Repository & Generate Artifacts

Below are the commands you’d run locally. They’ll produce the Dockerfile, Kubernetes YAMLs, and a GitHub Actions workflow file.

### 2.1 Detect Predominant Language

```bash
# Install the language detection tool (optional)
# npm install -g language-detection-tool

# Run the analysis
language-detection-tool --repo . --threshold 10
```

> **Result:**  
> The tool will output something like:

```
Predominant language: JavaScript (95%)
```

> If you don’t have a dedicated tool, you can use a simple heuristic: count the number of `.js`, `.ts`, `.py`, etc., files.

### 2.2 Create/Update Dockerfile

```bash
cat <<EOF > Dockerfile
# Base image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Maintainer
LABEL maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>"

# Working directory
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package files
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy source code
COPY . .

# Expose port
EXPOSE 3000

# Start command
CMD ["node", "index.js"]
EOF
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * Uses a lightweight Alpine‑based Node image.  
> * Installs only production dependencies (`npm ci --only=production`).  
> * Exposes port `3000` (adjust if your app listens elsewhere).  
> * Starts the app with `node index.js` (change if your entry point differs).

### 2.3 Generate Kubernetes YAMLs

Create a directory for manifests:

```bash
mkdir -p k8s
```

#### Deployment (`k8s/deployment.yaml`)

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
```

#### Service (`k8s/service.yaml`)

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **Notes**  
> * Adjust `replicas` if you want more or fewer pods.  
> * `image` should point to the registry where you’ll push the Docker image (e.g., GitHub Container Registry).  
> * `type: LoadBalancer` will provision an external IP on most cloud providers; change to `ClusterIP` or `NodePort` if you’re running locally.

### 2.4 Create GitHub Actions Workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/ci.yml`:

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Node.js
      uses: actions/setup-node@v4
      with:
        node-version: '18'

    - name: Install dependencies
      run: npm ci

    - name: Run tests
      run: npm test

    - name: Build Docker image
      run: |
        echo ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} | docker login ghcr.io -u ${{ github.actor }} --password-stdin
        docker build -t ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest .
        docker push ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest

    - name: Deploy to Kubernetes
      uses: azure/k8s-deploy@v4
      with:
        manifests: |
          k8s/deployment.yaml
          k8s/service.yaml
        images: |
          ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
        namespace: default
```

> **What this workflow does**  
> 1. Checks out the repo.  
> 2. Sets up Node 18.  
> 3. Installs dependencies and runs tests.  
> 4. Builds and pushes a Docker image to GitHub Container Registry.  
> 5. Deploys the new image to Kubernetes (requires a pre‑configured `k8s-deploy` action and cluster context).

> **Prerequisites**  
> * Add `GITHUB_TOKEN` secret (already available by default).  
> * Ensure the `azure/k8s-deploy` action has access to your cluster (you’ll need to set up a kubeconfig secret or use a self‑hosted runner).  
> * If you’re not deploying to Azure, replace the deploy step with the appropriate action for your provider.

---

## 3️⃣ Stage All Changes

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/*.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & Push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> **After pushing**  
> The GitHub Actions workflow will automatically trigger on the `push` event, building the Docker image, pushing it to GHCR, and deploying it to Kubernetes.

---

## Recap of What You’ll Have

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a lightweight Node image. |
| `k8s/deployment.yaml` | Deploys 3 replicas of your app. |
| `k8s/service.yaml` | Exposes the app via a LoadBalancer. |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | CI pipeline: test → build → push → deploy. |

Feel free to tweak any of the defaults (e.g., Node version, replica count, service type) to better fit your environment. If you hit any snags while setting this up, let me know and I’ll help troubleshoot!
